check.remediation: Set password creation requirements to conform to site policy. Many distributions provide tools for updating PAM configuration, consult your documentation for details. If no tooling is provided edit the appropriate /etc/pam.d/ configuration file and add or modify the pam_cracklib.so or pam_pwquality.so lines to include the required options: password required pam_cracklib.so try_first_pass retry=3 minlen=14 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 password requisite pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass retry=3 If pam_pwquality.so is in use also configure settings in /etc/security/pwquality.conf : minlen = 14 dcredit = -1 ucredit = -1 ocredit = -1 lcredit = -1 Notes: Consult your documentation for the appropriate PAM file and module. Additional module options may be set, recommendation requirements only cover including try_first_pass and minlen set to 14 or more. Settings in /etc/security/pwquality.conf must use spaces around the = symbol.
check.reason: Could not open file '/etc/pam.d/system-auth'

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure password reuse is limited.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure password reuse is limited.
check.description: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores the users' old passwords and can be checked to ensure that users are not recycling recent passwords.
check.rationale: Forcing users not to reuse their past 5 passwords make it less likely that an attacker will be able to guess the password. Note that these change only apply to accounts configured on the local system.
check.remediation: Set remembered password history to conform to site policy. Many distributions provide tools for updating PAM configuration, consult your documentation for details. If no tooling is provided edit the appropriate /etc/pam.d/ configuration file and add or modify the pam_pwhistory.so or pam_unix.so lines to include the remember option: password required pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 password sufficient pam_unix.so remember=5 Notes: Consult your documentation for the appropriate PAM file and module. Additional module options may be set, recommendation only covers those listed here.
check.reason: Could not open file '/etc/pam.d/system-auth'

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure password hashing algorithm is SHA-512.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure password hashing algorithm is SHA-512.
check.description: The commands below change password encryption from md5 to sha512 (a much stronger hashing algorithm). All existing accounts will need to perform a password change to upgrade the stored hashes to the new algorithm.
check.rationale: The SHA-512 algorithm provides much stronger hashing than MD5, thus providing additional protection to the system by increasing the level of effort for an attacker to successfully determine passwords. Note that these change only apply to accounts configured on the local system.
check.remediation: Set password hashing algorithm to sha512. Many distributions provide tools for updating PAM configuration, consult your documentation for details. If no tooling is provided edit the appropriate /etc/pam.d/ configuration file and add or modify the pam_unix.so lines to include the sha512 option: password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 Notes: Consult your documentation for the appropriate PAM file and module. Additional module options may be set, recommendation only covers those listed here. If it is determined that the password algorithm being used is not SHA-512, once it is changed, it is recommended that all user ID's be immediately expired and forced to change their passwords on next login. To accomplish that, the following commands can be used. Any system accounts that need to be expired should be carefully done separately by the system administrator to prevent any potential problems. # cat /etc/passwd | awk -F: '( $3 >= 500 && $1 != "nfsnobody" ) { print $1 }' | xargs -n 1 chage -d 0 This command assumes a system UID split at 500. Some distributions split at UID 1000 instead, consult your documentation and/or the UID_MIN setting in /etc/login.defs to determine which is appropriate for you.
check.reason: Could not open file '/etc/pam.d/system-auth'

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure password expiration is 365 days or less.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure password expiration is 365 days or less.
check.description: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to force passwords to expire once they reach a defined age. It is recommended that the PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter be set to less than or equal to 365 days.
check.rationale: The window of opportunity for an attacker to leverage compromised credentials or successfully compromise credentials via an online brute force attack is limited by the age of the password. Therefore, reducing the maximum age of a password also reduces an attacker's window of opportunity.
check.remediation: Set the PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter to conform to site policy in /etc/login.defs : PASS_MAX_DAYS 365 Modify user parameters for all users with a password set to match: # chage --maxdays 365 <user> Notes: You can also check this setting in /etc/shadow directly. The 5th field should be 365 or less for all users with a password. Note: A value of -1 will disable password expiration. Additionally the password expiration must be greater than the minimum days between password changes or users will be unable to change their password.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure minimum days between password changes is 7 or more.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure minimum days between password changes is 7 or more.
check.description: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have passed since the last time the user changed their password. It is recommended that PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter be set to 7 or more days.
check.rationale: By restricting the frequency of password changes, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls.
check.remediation: Set the PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter to 7 in /etc/login.defs : PASS_MIN_DAYS 7 Modify user parameters for all users with a password set to match: # chage --mindays 7 <user> Notes: You can also check this setting in /etc/shadow directly. The 4th field should be 7 or more for all users with a password.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure password expiration warning days is 7 or more.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure password expiration warning days is 7 or more.
check.description: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a defined number of days. It is recommended that the PASS_WARN_AGE parameter be set to 7 or more days.
check.rationale: Providing an advance warning that a password will be expiring gives users time to think of a secure password. Users caught unaware may choose a simple password or write it down where it may be discovered.
check.remediation: Set the PASS_WARN_AGE parameter to 7 in /etc/login.defs : PASS_WARN_AGE 7 Modify user parameters for all users with a password set to match: # chage --warndays 7 <user> Notes: You can also check this setting in /etc/shadow directly. The 6th field should be 7 or more for all users with a password.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure inactive password lock is 30 days or less.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure inactive password lock is 30 days or less.
check.description: User accounts that have been inactive for over a given period of time can be automatically disabled. It is recommended that accounts that are inactive for 30 days after password expiration be disabled.
check.rationale: Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security since the users are not logging in to notice failed login attempts or other anomalies.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set the default password inactivity period to 30 days: # useradd -D -f 30 Modify user parameters for all users with a password set to match: # chage --inactive 30 <user> Notes: You can also check this setting in /etc/shadow directly. The 7th field should be 30 or less for all users with a password. Note: A value of -1 would disable this setting.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure default group for the root account is GID 0.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure default group for the root account is GID 0.
check.description: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root user belongs to. This affects permissions of files that are created by the root user.
check.rationale: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent root -owned files from accidentally becoming accessible to non-privileged users.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set the root user default group to GID 0 : # usermod -g 0 root.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure access to the su command is restricted.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure access to the su command is restricted.
check.description: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo , which allows for more granular control over privileged access. Normally, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in /etc/pam.d/su , the su command will only allow users in the wheel group to execute su.
check.rationale: Restricting the use of su , and using sudo in its place, provides system administrators better control of the escalation of user privileges to execute privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and audit mechanism, as it can log each command executed via sudo , whereas su can only record that a user executed the su program.
check.remediation: Add the following line to the /etc/pam.d/su file: auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid Create a comma separated list of users in the wheel statement in the /etc/group file: wheel:x:10:root,<user list>.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/passwd are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/passwd are configured.
check.description: The /etc/passwd file contains user account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for these utilities to operate.
check.rationale: It is critical to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set permissions on /etc/passwd : # chown root:root /etc/passwd # chmod 644 /etc/passwd.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/shadow are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/shadow are configured.
check.description: The /etc/shadow file is used to store the information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
check.rationale: If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed password to break it. Other security information that is stored in the /etc/shadow file (such as expiration) could also be useful to subvert the user accounts.
check.remediation: Run the one of the following chown commands as appropriate and the chmod to set permissions on /etc/shadow : # chown root:root /etc/shadow # chown root:shadow /etc/shadow # chmod o-rwx,g-wx /etc/shadow.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/group are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/group are configured.
check.description: The /etc/group file contains a list of all the valid groups defined in the system. The command below allows read/write access for root and read access for everyone else.
check.rationale: The /etc/group file needs to be protected from unauthorized changes by non-privileged users, but needs to be readable as this information is used with many non-privileged programs.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set permissions on /etc/group : # chown root:root /etc/group # chmod 644 /etc/group.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured.
check.description: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store the information about groups that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
check.rationale: If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/gshadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed password to break it. Other security information that is stored in the /etc/gshadow file (such as group administrators) could also be useful to subvert the group.
check.remediation: Run the one of the following chown commands as appropriate and the chmod to set permissions on /etc/gshadow : # chown root:root /etc/gshadow # chown root:shadow /etc/gshadow # chmod o-rwx,g-rw /etc/gshadow.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured.
check.description: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
check.rationale: It is critical to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set permissions on /etc/passwd- : # chown root:root /etc/passwd- # chmod u-x,go-rwx /etc/passwd-.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured.
check.description: The /etc/shadow- file is used to store backup information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
check.rationale: It is critical to ensure that the /etc/shadow- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
check.remediation: Run the one of the following chown commands as appropriate and the chmod to set permissions on /etc/shadow- : # chown root:root /etc/shadow- # chown root:shadow /etc/shadow- # chmod o-rwx,g-rw /etc/shadow-.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/group- are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/group- are configured.
check.description: The /etc/group- file contains a backup list of all the valid groups defined in the system.
check.rationale: It is critical to ensure that the /etc/group- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
check.remediation: Run the following command to set permissions on /etc/group- : # chown root:root /etc/group- # chmod u-x,go-wx /etc/group-.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured.
check.description: The /etc/gshadow- file is used to store backup information about groups that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
check.rationale: It is critical to ensure that the /etc/gshadow- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
check.remediation: Run the one of the following chown commands as appropriate and the chmod to set permissions on /etc/gshadow- : # chown root:root /etc/gshadow- # chown root:shadow /etc/gshadow- # chmod o-rwx,g-rw /etc/gshadow-.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure password fields are not empty.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure password fields are not empty.
check.description: An account with an empty password field means that anybody may log in as that user without providing a password.
check.rationale: All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent the account from being used by an unauthorized user.
check.remediation: If any accounts in the /etc/shadow file do not have a password, run the following command to lock the account until it can be determined why it does not have a password: # passwd -l <username> Also, check to see if the account is logged in and investigate what it is being used for to determine if it needs to be forced off.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/passwd.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/passwd.
check.description: The character + in various files used to be markers for systems to insert data from NIS maps at a certain point in a system configuration file. These entries are no longer required on most systems, but may exist in files that have been imported from other platforms.
check.rationale: These entries may provide an avenue for attackers to gain privileged access on the system.
check.remediation: Remove any legacy '+' entries from /etc/passwd if they exist.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/shadow.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/shadow.
check.description: The character + in various files used to be markers for systems to insert data from NIS maps at a certain point in a system configuration file. These entries are no longer required on most systems, but may exist in files that have been imported from other platforms.
check.rationale: These entries may provide an avenue for attackers to gain privileged access on the system.
check.remediation: Remove any legacy '+' entries from /etc/shadow if they exist.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/group.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no legacy '+' entries exist in /etc/group.
check.description: The character + in various files used to be markers for systems to insert data from NIS maps at a certain point in a system configuration file. These entries are no longer required on most systems, but may exist in files that have been imported from other platforms.
check.rationale: These entries may provide an avenue for attackers to gain privileged access on the system.
check.remediation: Remove any legacy '+' entries from /etc/group if they exist.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure root is the only UID 0 account.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure root is the only UID 0 account.
check.description: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
check.rationale: This access must be limited to only the default root account and only from the system console. Administrative access must be through an unprivileged account using an approved mechanism as noted in Item 5.6 Ensure access to the su command is restricted.
check.remediation: Remove any users other than root with UID 0 or assign them a new UID if appropriate.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure root PATH Integrity.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure root PATH Integrity.
check.description: The root user can execute any command on the system and could be fooled into executing programs unintentionally if the PATH is not set correctly.
check.rationale: Including the current working directory (.) or other writable directory in root 's executable path makes it likely that an attacker can gain superuser access by forcing an administrator operating as root to execute a Trojan horse program.
check.remediation: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure all groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure all groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group.
check.description: Over time, system administration errors and changes can lead to groups being defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group.
check.rationale: Groups defined in the /etc/passwd file but not in the /etc/group file pose a threat to system security since group permissions are not properly managed.
check.remediation: Analyze the output of the Audit step above and perform the appropriate action to correct any discrepancies found.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist.
check.description: Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate User ID (UID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the UID field.
check.rationale: Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.
check.remediation: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique UIDs and review all files owned by the shared UIDs to determine which UID they are supposed to belong to.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist.
check.description: Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate Group ID (GID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the GID field.
check.rationale: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.
check.remediation: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique GIDs and review all files owned by the shared GID to determine which group they are supposed to belong to. Notes: You can also use the grpck command to check for other inconsistencies in the /etc/group file.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no duplicate user names exist.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no duplicate user names exist.
check.description: Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate user name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the user name.
check.rationale: If a user is assigned a duplicate user name, it will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd . For example, if "test4" has a UID of 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has a UID of 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. Effectively, the UID is shared, which is a security problem.
check.remediation: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique user names for the users. File ownerships will automatically reflect the change as long as the users have unique UIDs.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure no duplicate group names exist.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure no duplicate group names exist.
check.description: Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate group name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the group name.
check.rationale: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and have access to files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group . Effectively, the GID is shared, which is a security problem.
check.remediation: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique names for the user groups. File group ownerships will automatically reflect the change as long as the groups have unique GIDs.

rule.description: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.: Ensure shadow group is empty.

sca.policy: CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark v2.0.0.

check.title: Ensure shadow group is empty.
check.description: The shadow group allows system programs which require access the ability to read the /etc/shadow file. No users should be assigned to the shadow group.
check.rationale: Any users assigned to the shadow group would be granted read access to the /etc/shadow file. If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed passwords to break them. Other security information that is stored in the /etc/shadow file (such as expiration) could also be useful to subvert additional user accounts.
check.remediation: Remove all users from the shadow group, and change the primary group of any users with shadow as their primary group.
